title: Rust
text:
Introduction: Why Rust Matters
For decades, systems programming forced engineers into an uncomfortable compromise:

Control and Speed without Safety: Languages like C and C++ provide bare-metal hardware access, deterministic resource destruction, and peak performance, but leave memory safety, thread safety, and undefined behavior to developer discipline. Decades of CVE audits prove that even the most disciplined teams cannot prevent memory corruption at scale.
Safety without Bare-Metal Control: Managed languages like Java, Go, Python, and C# enforce memory safety through automatic garbage collection and runtime checks. However, garbage collection introduces non-deterministic pause times, memory footprint overhead, and indirection that make them less suitable for low-latency systems, kernel drivers, game engines, and embedded microcontrollers.

Rust breaks this compromise by achieving compile-time memory safety without a garbage collector.

The Problem Rust Solves
Software reliability and security crises predominantly stem from memory safety bugs and concurrency defects: - Spatial memory safety violations: Buffer overruns, out-of-bounds array reads and writes. - Temporal memory safety violations: Use-after-free, double free, dangling pointers. - Concurrency bugs: Data races occurring when two threads access the same memory location concurrently with at least one writer and no synchronization.
Rust guarantees that properly written safe code cannot experience any of these defects. If your code compiles, these failure modes are mathematically disproven by the compiler’s borrow checker.


How Rust Achieves This
Rust replaces runtime garbage collection and manual memory management with three core mechanisms: 1. Ownership: Every value has a single owner bound to lexical scope. When the owner goes out of scope, the memory is deterministically freed (Drop). 2. Borrowing & References: References allow inspection or mutation of data without taking ownership. Rust enforces aliasing XOR mutability at compile time: you may have either any number of immutable references (&T) or exactly one mutable reference (&mut T), but never both simultaneously. 3. Lifetimes: The compiler tracks the validity of every reference, preventing dangling pointers across function boundaries and data structures at compile time without runtime overhead.


What You Will Learn
Across 20 comprehensive chapters and three end-to-end production capstones, this book covers: - Core language syntax, primitive/compound types, and zero-cost control flow. - Deep mechanical mastery of ownership, stack vs. heap allocation, move semantics, and lifetimes. - Robust data modeling with algebraic data types (struct, enum) and expressive pattern matching. - Explicit, resilient error handling with Result, Option, and the ? propagation operator. - Parametric polymorphism with generics, trait bounds, and dynamic dispatch via trait objects. - Fearless concurrency using threads, message-passing channels, and atomic primitives. - Asynchronous programming with async/await, Future, and the Tokio runtime. - Systems-level metaprogramming with declarative macros, procedural macros, and foreign function interfaces (FFI). - Production engineering: profiling, benchmarking with Criterion, Criterion, cargo packaging, WebAssembly (wasm-pack), and embedded no_std firmware.


How to Read This Book

Linear Progression: Chapters 1 through 13 form the core foundation. Read them sequentially; each chapter relies strictly on concepts verified in preceding sections.
Complete, Runnable Code: Every listing is self-contained. Copy the code into your editor, compile it with cargo check and cargo run, and observe compiler messages.
Fight and Befriend the Borrow Checker: When the compiler rejects your code, read the compiler diagnostic carefully. Rust diagnostics are world-class teaching tools explaining what invariant was violated and how to rectify it.
Capstones & Projects: Work through the three integrated projects (CLI Task Manager, Parallel Data Pipeline with Rayon, and Async HTTP API with Axum and SQLx) to solidify architecture and integration patterns.



The Current State of Rust
Rust is mature, battle-tested, and officially adopted across industry leaders for core infrastructure: - The Linux kernel has official support for Rust drivers and kernel modules. - Major cloud hypervisors and networking layers (AWS Firecracker, Cloudflare Workers, Android OS) are authored in Rust. - Standards organizations and government agencies (CISA, NSA) recommend transitioning memory-unsafe codebases to memory-safe languages like Rust.


What Rust Is Not
To set clear expectations, Rust is not: - An object-oriented language with class hierarchies: Rust uses composition, traits, and algebraic data types rather than inheritance. - A rapid prototyping scripting language: Rust demands explicit thinking up front about ownership, error conditions, and data lifetimes. - Magic: Zero-cost abstractions mean you don’t pay runtime costs for high-level ergonomics; however, you must understand machine layouts and memory representation.

Installing Rust with rustup
The primary and official method for installing and managing Rust toolchains across all platforms is rustup.

Installing rustup
On Linux and macOS, install rustup via your terminal:
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh
Follow the default prompts. This installs: - rustc: The Rust compiler. - cargo: The package manager and build system. - rustup: The toolchain multiplexer. - rust-std: Standard library binaries for your host architecture.


Managing Toolchains
Configure your shell environment:
source "$HOME/.cargo/env"
rustc --version
cargo --version
To update your toolchain to the latest stable release:
rustup update stable

Your First Program: Hello World
Let’s begin with the canonical starting point: a minimal standalone Rust source file.

Direct Compilation with rustc
Create a file named main.rs:
// main.rs
fn main() {
    println!("Hello, world!");
}
Compile and run directly using rustc:
rustc main.rs
./main
Output:
Hello, world!


Deconstructing the Program

fn main() { ... }: The main function is the entry point of every executable Rust program. It takes no arguments and returns unit ().
println!(...): In Rust, names ending in an exclamation mark ! invoke macros rather than standard functions. println! parses format strings at compile time to ensure type safety.

The Role of Cargo
Cargo handles four essential engineering responsibilities: 1. Dependency Resolution: Downloading, pinning, and compiling external crates from crates.io. 2. Build Orchestration: Invoking rustc with optimal optimization flags, link arguments, and target settings. 3. cargo build   # Compile debug build with symbols into target/debug

Stack vs Heap Memory in Rust
text:
Stack vs Heap Memory in Rust
Understanding where data lives is essential for writing efficient Rust code.

The Stack

Fast, LIFO (Last In, First Out) allocation.
All data stored on the stack must have a known, fixed size at compile time.
Primitive types, fixed arrays, and function frames live on the stack.



The Heap

Dynamic memory allocated at runtime.
The operating system locates a contiguous region of memory, marks it in use, and returns a pointer.
Slower than stack allocation; requires dereferencing pointers.
Dynamically sized types like String and Vec<T> store metadata on the stack (pointer, length, capacity) pointing to heap buffers.

title: The Cost of Drop on Deep Ownership Chains
text:
Thesis
Drop is not free. A long chain of Box nodes runs destructors one by one; mem::forget skips them and returns in nanoseconds — which is also how you leak. This chapter times dropping chains of 1 k / 10 k / 100 k nodes versus forgetting the large chain.

title: The Cost of Drop on Deep Ownership Chains
text:
Mental model
  drop(head) → Drop::drop → drop(child) → …  (recursive / iterative cleanup)
  mem::forget(head) → no destructors; memory leaked unless into a global allocator you never reclaim

title: The Cost of Drop on Deep Ownership Chains
text:
Worked examples
Verified with rustc 1.99.1, cargo run --release.
// chain of Box<Node>; time drop vs forget
Output:
drop chain of    1000 nodes: 21.888µs
drop chain of   10000 nodes: 267.357µs
drop chain of  100000 nodes: 4.211461ms
forget chain of  100000 nodes: 487ns
Drop scales with chain length (~4 ms for 100 k nodes here). forget on the same shape was ~0.5 µs — and leaked the graph.

title: Shared and Mutable References
The Borrowing Rules Demystified
text:
The Borrowing Rules Demystified
Rust’s compiler enforces two fundamental rules regarding references at compile time:

At any given time, you can have either one mutable reference or any number of immutable references.
References must always be valid.


Why the Rules Exist
This rule (often summarized as Aliasing XOR Mutability) prevents data races. A data race occurs when: - Two or more pointers access the same memory concurrently. - At least one pointer is writing. - There is no synchronization.
By disallowing simultaneous reading and writing through multiple aliases, Rust eliminates data races before the code ever compiles.

title: if-let Guards and cfg_select!
text:
Thesis
Rust 1.95 stabilised two small features that remove a lot of everyday boilerplate:

if-let guards let a match arm bind and test in its guard: Pat if let Some(x) = f(y) && x > 0 => …. If the guard fails, matching falls through to the next arm, just like a plain if guard.
cfg_select! is a compile-time match over cfg predicates. The first arm whose predicate is true is expanded, and _ is the fallback. It does the job the cfg-if crate has done for years, with no dependency.

Both have one sharp edge. The compiler doesn’t count guards towards exhaustiveness, and a cfg_select! where no arm is true is a hard error.

title: if-let Guards and cfg_select!
text:
Mental model



A match with if-let guards tries arm 1 (pattern matches, guard false, fall through), then arm 2 (guard true, body runs with both bindings); an unguarded arm is still needed for exhaustiveness. cfg_select! expands the first true cfg arm at compile time


An if-let guard runs after the arm’s pattern has matched. It can use the pattern’s bindings, introduce new ones, and chain more conditions with && (the same let-chain grammar that was stabilised for if in Rust 1.88). The new bindings are in scope only in that arm’s body. If any part of the chain fails, those bindings are dropped and the next arm is tried.

title: if-let Guards and cfg_select!
if-let Guards and cfg_select!
if-let Guards and cfg_select!
text:
Migrating from cfg-if
The cfg-if crate’s if #[cfg(unix)] { … } else if #[cfg(windows)] { … } else { … } maps one to one onto cfg_select! { unix => { … } windows => { … } _ => { … } }. Before you drop the dependency, check two things:

MSRV. cfg_select! needs Rust 1.95. If you publish a library with a lower rust-version, keep cfg-if until you raise it.
Expression position. cfg-if only expands to items. cfg_select! also works as an expression, so let x = cfg_select! { … }; replaces the common #[cfg] + #[cfg(not)] pair of let statements.

text: The Never Type ! and Infallible

title: The Never Type ! and Infallible
text:
Thesis
Rust has always had a type for “this expression does not produce a value”: !, the never type. panic!(), loop {} without break, return, continue, and std::process::exit all have type !, and a function declared -> ! promises never to return. Until now you could only write ! in that return position. Everywhere else — Result<T, !>, type Error = !;, impl Trait for ! — it was an unstable feature, and the standard library used a stand-in, the empty enum std::convert::Infallible.
Rust 1.100 (scheduled for 2026-11-12) stabilizes ! as an ordinary type after a decade behind a feature gate, and makes Infallible a plain alias for it. The language change is small; the error-handling consequence is real: “this operation cannot fail” now has one canonical spelling, Result<T, !>, that the compiler understands well enough to let you skip the impossible Err arm entirely.
The same release changes never type fallback to ! on every edition, which is a small breaking change for code that quietly relied on the old fallback to (). This chapter shows both sides, compiled with the current beta and stable toolchains.

title: The Never Type ! and Infallible
text:
Mental model
            ┌──────────────────── every type ────────────────────┐
            │   u32   String   ()   Vec<T>   Result<T, E>   …   │
            └───────────────────────────▲─────────────────────────┘
                                        │  coerces to any type
                                        │  (unreachable code needs no value)
                                       `!`   — no values at all

Result<T, !>   =  Ok(T) | Err(<impossible>)      → only Ok can exist
size_of::<Result<u32, !>>() == size_of::<u32>()  → no discriminant needed
Infallible     =  !   (type alias since 1.100)
Three facts carry the whole chapter:







Fact
Consequence




! has no values
Code that “holds” one is unreachable; the compiler can delete branches that need it


! coerces to any type
A diverging arm (die(…), panic!, return) fits in a match whose other arms are u32


An enum variant containing ! is uninhabited
let Ok(v) = r; is irrefutable when r: Result<T, !>; the Err arm need not be written



Infallible was the library’s way to get the same effect (an enum with no variants). Since it is now literally !, existing APIs such as TryFrom implementations whose error is Infallible work unchanged and read the same way.

title: The Never Type ! and Infallible
text:
The trap
Relying on inference to pick () for you. Code like f()?;, run(|| panic!()), or if c { Default::default() } else { return } compiled for years because the never type quietly became () when nothing else constrained it. Under 1.100 (any edition) or edition 2024 that guess is !, and the code either fails to compile — the good case, shown above — or, in the rare unsafe case the never_type_fallback_flowing_into_unsafe lint exists for, picks a different type than the author assumed. The compiler’s 1.99 lint (dependency_on_unit_never_type_fallback) points at every affected function: fix those before you bump the toolchain, not after.
The second, quieter trap is using ! as a placeholder in a public trait impl or function signature because “it can’t fail today”. ! is a promise. Replacing it with a real error type later breaks every caller who wrote let Ok(v) = …;.

title: The Never Type ! and Infallible
text:
The boring rule
Use -> ! for functions that truly never return and Result<T, !> (or Infallible until your MSRV is 1.100) only where failure is impossible by construction. Never lean on fallback: when the compiler cannot see a type, write it — f::<()>()?, || -> () { … }, () = expr;. Turn on the rust_2024_compatibility lints on older editions and clear them before upgrading.

title: Generic Const Arguments (GCA)
text:
Thesis
On stable Rust, a const generic parameter may appear in a const argument alone ([u8; N]) or as a fully concrete expression ([u8; 1 + 1]). The moment you write [u8; N + 1] or [u8; T::ASSOC], the compiler stops you. The old escape hatch, #![feature(generic_const_exprs)] (GCE), taught everyone the shape of the problem but never became a stabilization candidate.
Generic Const Arguments (GCA) is the Const Generics project group’s replacement family of nightly features. Expressions that involve generic parameters go through an explicit gca!(…) marker (for now), each capability has its own gate (gca_adts, gca_min_const_items, gca_const_items, …), and definitional equality — not GCE’s evaluation model — decides when two const arguments match. Nothing here is stable. This chapter shows what compiles on today’s nightly, marks every feature gate, and records where the Oct 2026 blog post already drifted from the compiler.
Version note: verified on rustc 1.101.0-nightly (a30aa9064 2026-10-08). The Inside Rust post Generic Const Args and You (2026-10-02) is the design overview; on this nightly the feature formerly named generic_const_args has been renamed to gca_const_items (removed name errors say “removed in 1.100.0”), and the gca! macro lives at std::gca / core::gca. No RFC yet; the project group says polish first.
Stable const generics basics (structs/functions parameterized by const N: usize) live in Generic Functions and Data Structures. This chapter does not re-teach that.

title: Generic Const Arguments (GCA)
text:
Mental model
Stable today
  const arg ::=  N  |  <fully concrete expr>
                 └── generic param alone

GCE (legacy nightly)     — evaluate complex exprs; hard to stabilize
GCA (current nightly)    — mark exprs with gca!(…); equality by definition
       │
       ├── gca_adts              arrays / tuples / structs / enums in gca!(…)
       ├── gca_min_const_items   const items whose RHS is gca!(…)
       ├── gca_const_items       + opaque const items, assoc bindings, dyn, needs -Znext-solver often
       └── gca_macroless_*       experimental: insert gca!(…) for you (rough)







Fact
Consequence




gca!(…) may mention generic parameters
Plain { N + 1 } as a const argument still cannot

gca!(N + 1) and gca!(foo()) are not automatically legal; prefer const items / ADTs that the gates support


gca_const_items requires gca_min_const_items

title: PhantomData and the Type-State Pattern: Protocol States the Compiler Enforces
text:
Thesis
A lot of APIs have an order to them: connect, then log in, then query. Most libraries check that order at runtime, with a state field and an Err(NotConnected) when it’s wrong. Rust can check it at compile time instead. Make the state a type parameter, give each state its own impl block, and have every transition take self by value and return the next state. Calling a method in the wrong state is then a type error. Reusing an old state is a use-after-move error.
The part that makes this work is std::marker::PhantomData<S>. It is a zero-sized field that “uses” the type parameter without storing anything. This chapter builds a small type-state connection, shows the compiler errors it produces, measures what it costs at runtime (nothing), and covers the one decision you have to get right: which PhantomData.



Type-state transitions for Conn, the compile errors they produce, their size, and the marker choice


All listings were compiled with rustc 1.99.1, edition 2024.

title: PhantomData and the Type-State Pattern: Protocol States the Compiler Enforces
section: Why you need PhantomData at all
text:
Why you need PhantomData at all
Rust rejects a type parameter that no field mentions:
struct Conn<S> { host: String }
error[E0392]: type parameter `S` is never used
 --> bad3.rs:1:13
  |
1 | struct Conn<S> { host: String }
  |             ^ unused type parameter
  |
  = help: consider removing `S`, referring to it in a field, or using a marker such as `PhantomData`
  = help: if you intended `S` to be a const parameter, use `const S: /* Type */` instead

error: aborting due to 1 previous error

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0392`.
The error is deliberate. The compiler needs to know how Conn<S> relates to S for variance, drop checking and auto traits (Send/Sync). PhantomData<T> answers that question by saying “act as if this struct holds a T” (std docs), while taking zero bytes.

title: PhantomData and the Type-State Pattern: Protocol States the Compiler Enforces
text:
Choosing the right PhantomData
PhantomData<S> says “I own an S”, so Conn<S> takes on S’s auto traits. That matters if a state marker happens to be !Send, even though no S value ever exists:
use std::marker::PhantomData;
use std::rc::Rc;

// A state marker that happens to be !Send (it is never constructed).
#[allow(dead_code)]
struct Local(Rc<()>);

struct Owns<S>(PhantomData<S>);          // "acts like it owns an S"
struct Tag<S>(PhantomData<fn() -> S>);   // "only names S": Send + Sync, covariant

fn assert_send<T: Send>() {}

fn main() {
    assert_send::<Tag<Local>>();
    assert_send::<Owns<Local>>();
}
error[E0277]: `Rc<()>` cannot be sent between threads safely
  --> auto.rs:15:19
   |
15 |     assert_send::<Owns<Local>>();
   |                   ^^^^^^^^^^^ `Rc<()>` cannot be sent between threads safely
   |
   = help: within `Owns<Local>`, the trait `Send` is not implemented for `Rc<()>`
note: required because it appears within the type `Local`
  --> auto.rs:6:8
   |
 6 | struct Local(Rc<()>);
   |        ^^^^^
note: required because it appears within the type `PhantomData<Local>`
  --> /rustc/58cf8f9c35b355199727627d07ae34a4e2846d67/library/core/src/marker.rs:811:11
note: required because it appears within the type `Owns<Local>`
  --> auto.rs:8:8
   |
 8 | struct Owns<S>(PhantomData<S>);          // "acts like it owns an S"
   |        ^^^^
note: required by a bound in `assert_send`
  --> auto.rs:11:19
   |
11 | fn assert_send<T: Send>() {}
   |                   ^^^^ required by this bound in `assert_send`

error: aborting due to 1 previous error

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0277`.
Tag<Local> compiles and Owns<Local> does not. The Rustonomicon’s PhantomData table lists the options:

For type-state markers, where S is only a label, PhantomData<fn() -> S> is usually the most accurate choice. The struct never owns an S, so it shouldn’t inherit S’s thread-safety or drop behaviour. Use plain PhantomData<S> when the struct really does own S values in a way the compiler can’t see, such as a raw-pointer collection, because that is what keeps drop checking sound.

title: PhantomData and the Type-State Pattern: Protocol States the Compiler Enforces
text:
When not to use type-state

The state comes from runtime data. If the server decides whether you’re authenticated, you still need Result at the boundary, as login shows. You can’t hold a Vec of connections in different states without an enum or a trait object, so mixed collections go back to runtime state.
There are many states and many shared methods. Every state you add means another impl block and more generic signatures. More than four or five states is usually a sign you want an enum.
The API is public and stable. Each state type becomes part of your public API, and renaming one is a breaking change.

title: PhantomData and the Type-State Pattern: Protocol States the Compiler Enforces
text:
Takeaways

A type parameter plus PhantomData turns protocol order into type checking, with zero runtime cost (48 bytes in every state, measured).
Transitions consume self. A failed transition returns the old state in Err.
Out-of-order calls become E0599 and reuse becomes E0382, both at compile time.
Pick the marker on purpose: PhantomData<fn() -> S> for pure labels, PhantomData<S> only when you logically own an S.

title: The Newtype Pattern: Zero-Cost Type Safety, Validated Values and the Orphan Rule
text:
Thesis
A newtype is a tuple struct with one field: struct AccountId(u64);. It costs nothing at runtime, because it has the same size and alignment as what it wraps, but it is a different type to the compiler. That one property gives you three tools:

Values with the same representation can no longer be mixed up. Account IDs, amounts, metres and seconds all stop being “just a u64”.
A private field plus a validating constructor means that holding the type is proof the value was checked.
A local wrapper lets you implement a foreign trait for a foreign type, which the orphan rule otherwise forbids.

This chapter demonstrates each one with compiler output from rustc 1.99.1, and shows where #[repr(transparent)] becomes necessary rather than optional.



The newtype pattern: one field, a new name, zero runtime cost

Pitfalls

Deref as inheritance. impl Deref<Target = String> for Email makes email.len() work, but it also adds every String method to the Email API, and email.to_uppercase() quietly returns a plain String. Implement AsRef<str> and the few methods you actually mean.
DerefMut breaks validation. It lets callers write *email = "junk".into() and skip TryFrom altogether.
pub fields remove validation the same way (section 3).
Boilerplate. Each trait you want, such as Display, FromStr, serde, or arithmetic for units, has to be derived or forwarded. #[derive] covers the standard traits, and #[serde(transparent)] serialises the newtype as its inner value. Write impls by hand where the semantics differ, as with Cents * Cents.

title: What Lifetimes Are (and Are Not)
text:
What Lifetimes Are (and Are Not)
Every reference in Rust has a lifetime—the scope for which that reference is valid.

What Lifetimes Are Not

Lifetimes do not change how long a value lives at runtime.
Lifetimes do not allocate or free memory.
Lifetimes are purely compile-time annotations that help the borrow checker ensure references never outlive the data they point to.

title: The Lifetime Elision Rules
text:
The Lifetime Elision Rules
In common function patterns, Rust automatically infers lifetime parameters via three elision rules:

Each parameter that is a reference gets its own lifetime parameter (fn foo<'a, 'b>(x: &'a i32, y: &'b i32)).
If there is exactly one input lifetime parameter, that lifetime is assigned to all output lifetime parameters (fn foo<'a>(x: &'a i32) -> &'a i32).
If there are multiple input lifetime parameters, but one of them is &self or &mut self, the lifetime of self is assigned to all output lifetime parameters.

title: Variance: Why &mut Makes Lifetimes Rigid
text:
Thesis
Most lifetime errors that look like “the borrow checker is being stubborn” are really about variance. Variance is the rule that decides when a type with a longer lifetime can be used where a shorter one is expected. A &'static str can be passed anywhere a &'a str is wanted, but a &mut &'static str can’t be passed where a &mut &'a str is wanted. The reason isn’t arbitrary: if it were allowed, safe code could put a dangling reference into a 'static slot.
This chapter shows the three kinds of variance in compiler output, explains why each one has to be that way, and then works through the most common real bug variance causes: the &'a mut self signature that locks a struct for the rest of its life.



Covariant, invariant and contravariant positions, with ’static outliving ’short


All listings were compiled with rustc 1.99.1, edition 2024. Every error message shown is the compiler’s actual output.

title: Variance: Why &mut Makes Lifetimes Rigid
text:
Subtyping, but only for lifetimes
Rust has no struct inheritance, so the only subtyping is between lifetimes. If 'long outlives 'short (written 'long: 'short), then &'long T is a subtype of &'short T, and a value of the first type can be used where the second is expected (Reference: Subtyping and Variance).
Variance describes how that relationship carries through a type constructor F<T>:

Covariant: if A is a subtype of B, then F<A> is a subtype of F<B>. The relationship carries through unchanged.
Invariant: F<A> and F<B> are unrelated unless A and B are the same type.
Contravariant: the relationship flips, so F<B> is a subtype of F<A>.

title: Variance: Why &mut Makes Lifetimes Rigid
text:
Pitfalls

Assuming Cell is “just a wrapper”. Adding a Cell<&'a T> field to a struct that used to be covariant makes it invariant. That is a breaking change for downstream code that relied on shrinking lifetimes, even though no public signature changed.
Reaching for 'static to “fix” invariance errors. Writing T: 'static or &'static everywhere makes the error go away by making the API useless for borrowed data. Find the &mut or Cell that forces invariance instead.
Reading E0499 or E0502 at face value. “Mutably borrowed in the previous iteration of the loop” on a method call usually means the method’s signature ties &mut self to a struct lifetime. Check the signature before you restructure the loop.
Unsafe code with the wrong variance. A raw-pointer container that stores *const T is covariant, but if it hands out &mut T it probably needs to be invariant. Variance mistakes in unsafe code are soundness bugs, not just inconvenient compile errors.

title: Variance: Why &mut Makes Lifetimes Rigid
text:
Takeaways

Shared references are covariant, so longer lifetimes shrink to fit.
Anything you can write through (&mut T, Cell<T>, *mut T) is invariant in T, because otherwise safe code could store a dangling reference.
Function arguments are contravariant, so callbacks that accept more are acceptable where callbacks that accept less are expected.
A struct’s variance comes from its fields, so changing a field type can be a breaking change.
&'a mut Thing<'a> locks Thing for its whole lifetime. Let the &mut self borrow have its own lifetime.

LazyLock and OnceLock
Global or shared values often need one-time initialization: a compiled regex, a config snapshot, a connection pool handle. Before Rust 1.70 / 1.80 you reached for lazy_static, once_cell, or a hand-rolled Mutex<Option<T>>. Today the standard library covers the boring cases:
Prefer LazyLock for static values with a pure init function. Prefer OnceLock when initialization needs arguments, fallible setup, or happens explicitly in main / a builder. This chapter sits next to Mutex and Arc because the shared handle is often wrapped in those types later — but lazy init itself is not a lock around every read after the first.

title: LazyLock and OnceLock
text:
Mental model
first access / set()
        │
        ▼
  run init exactly once  ──►  store T
        │
        ▼
 later access  ──►  &T (no re-init)

Concurrent first accessors: one wins the init; others wait, then see the same T.
If the init closure panics, LazyLock is poisoned for the rest of the process (unrecoverable). Fail fallible work before installing into a LazyLock, or use OnceLock + Result you control.
static LazyLock<T> values are not dropped at process exit; the OS reclaims the memory. That is intentional and fine for process-lifetime data.

title: MaybeUninit and Uninitialized Memory
text:
MaybeUninit and Uninitialized Memory
Safe Rust assumes every value is valid for its type: a bool is only true or false, a reference is non-null and aligned, a Vec<T> upholds its length/capacity invariants. Sometimes you need storage before those invariants hold — out-pointers, element-by-element arrays, FFI buffers. The standard tool is std::mem::MaybeUninit<T>: a wrapper that tells the compiler “these bytes might not be initialized yet.”
Do not reach for the deprecated mem::uninitialized or casual mem::zeroed on arbitrary T. Prefer MaybeUninit, initialize deliberately, then assume_init only when every validity requirement of T is met.

text:
Mental model
MaybeUninit::uninit()     ← bytes may be garbage; Drop of T does NOT run
        │
   write / ptr::write     ← initialize without dropping old (uninit) contents
        │
 assume_init / assume_init_drop
        │
        ▼
       T                  ← normal Drop and safe APIs apply







API
Role




MaybeUninit::uninit()
Allocate storage; contents uninitialized


MaybeUninit::new(v)
Already-initialized wrapper


MaybeUninit::zeroed()
Fill with 0 bytes — only valid if all-zero is a valid T


write(val)
Initialize (overwrites without dropping previous)


assume_init()
Assert fully initialized; take ownership as T


assume_init_drop()
Drop in place when you do not want ownership


as_mut_ptr() / &raw mut (*ptr).field
Field-by-field init without creating &mut to uninit fields



Dropping a MaybeUninit<T> never runs T’s destructor. If you initialized and then abandon the wrapper without assume_init / assume_init_drop, you leak resources (safe but usually undesirable).

title: Custom Allocators and the Allocator API
text:
Thesis
Every Box and Vec you have written so far got its memory from one place: the global allocator. You could swap that allocator for the whole program with #[global_allocator], but you could not say “this vector lives in that arena”. The Allocator trait that would let you do so has existed since 2016, behind the nightly-only allocator_api feature, and arena crates have shipped nightly-only allocator-aware APIs for years because of it.
Rust 1.100 (scheduled for 2026-11-12) stabilizes a deliberately small slice of that design: the std::alloc::Allocator trait, the Global and System allocators as implementors, and allocator-aware constructors on exactly two containers, Box<T, A> and Vec<T, A>. Everything else (Rc::new_in, fallible try_*_in constructors, allocator-aware String and HashMap) stays unstable under a new feature name, allocator_ext.
This chapter builds two allocators on the stable surface, a counting wrapper and a bump arena. It then walks through the places where the type system and the abort-on-failure policy catch people out. Everything was compiled with the current beta, which is what becomes 1.100.

title: Custom Allocators and the Allocator API
text:
Mental model
                 Vec<T, A>  /  Box<T, A>          (A defaults to Global)
                        │  holds an A by value
                        ▼
   ┌──────────────────── unsafe trait Allocator ─────────────────────┐
   │ allocate(&self, Layout)        -> Result<NonNull<[u8]>, AllocError>
   │ deallocate(&self, NonNull<u8>, Layout)            (unsafe)
   │ grow / grow_zeroed / shrink / allocate_zeroed     (provided)
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          ▲                 ▲                    ▲
        Global            System           your type, or &YourType
   (#[global_allocator]) (the OS heap)     (arena, pool, counter…)
Four facts carry the chapter:







Fact
Consequence




The allocator is a type parameter with a default: Vec<T, A = Global>
Vec<u32> and Vec<u32, System> are different types. Code written for one does not accept the other


The container stores an A
A zero-sized allocator (Global, System) costs nothing; &Arena costs one pointer; &dyn Allocator costs two


Methods take &self
Implement Allocator on &Arena (blanket impl provided) to share one arena among many containers. Interior mutability (Cell) does the bookkeeping


The trait is unsafe to implement
You promise that returned blocks are valid until deallocated, that blocks don’t overlap, and that no method unwinds. The compiler cannot check any of it



allocate returns NonNull<[u8]>, a slice pointer, so an allocator can report that it handed back more than was asked for. AllocError is a zero-sized “no” with no further detail.

title: Fast Float Reductions: Algebraic Operations vs Explicit Lanes
text:
Fast Float Reductions: Algebraic Operations vs Explicit Lanes
After this page you can explain why iter().map(|(x, y)| x * y).sum() over f32 runs as a slow scalar loop even at -O3, speed it up with the algebraic_* float methods stabilized in Rust 1.98, and decide when to write explicit accumulator lanes instead. Both run at about the same speed, but only the lanes give the same bits on every build.

title: Fast Float Reductions: Algebraic Operations vs Explicit Lanes
text:
Thesis
IEEE 754 addition isn’t associative, so (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) can round differently. Rust’s + on floats promises the exact IEEE result of the expression as written. That forbids the reordering a vectorizer needs, so a float reduction becomes one long dependency chain. f32::algebraic_add/algebraic_mul (and _sub, _div, _rem, likewise on f64) lift that promise per operation. The standard library docs say they “allow the compiler to optimize floating point operations using all the usual algebraic properties of real numbers,” and also that “algebraic operations are non-deterministic.” You get the speed and give up reproducibility. Writing the reassociation yourself gets you the speed and keeps reproducibility.

title: Fast Float Reductions: Algebraic Operations vs Explicit Lanes
text:
Mental model



Strict addition is one serial chain emitted as scalar addss; algebraic_add lets the compiler build vector partial sums but the result varies with opt level and target; explicit lanes vectorize too and give identical bits everywhere


The docs’ own example is that a.algebraic_add(b).algebraic_add(c).algebraic_add(d) may be computed as written or as (a + c) + (b + d). The rewrites allowed are deliberately unspecified. Typically they include reassociation, contraction into fused multiply-add, replacing division with reciprocal multiplication, and ignoring the sign of zero. NaN, ±Inf and -0.0 “may behave in unexpected ways.” The results are always valid floats and never undefined behavior, but unsafe code must not depend on any property of them.

title: Fast Float Reductions: Algebraic Operations vs Explicit Lanes
Fast Float Reductions: Algebraic Operations vs Explicit Lanes
text:
Choosing between them







Need
Use




Bit-identical results across builds, targets and runs (tests with exact expectations, consensus, replay, deterministic simulation)
strict +, or explicit lanes when you need speed


Fastest reduction in a hot loop, tolerance-based checks, results that may differ between machines
algebraic_*


A specific vector width or FMA on purpose
explicit lanes, or f32::mul_add (which is exact fused multiply-add, not “maybe”)



The algebraic methods are opt-in per operation. Unlike C’s -ffast-math, they don’t change the semantics of every float operation in the crate, and they don’t add -ffinite-math-only’s assumption that NaNs and infinities never occur, the assumption that lets a compiler delete isnan checks. Only the operations you mark can be rewritten.

title: Fast Float Reductions: Algebraic Operations vs Explicit Lanes
text:
Things that bite

assert_eq! on an algebraic result is a flaky test. The docs say two evaluations of the same expression may differ “even within a single program run.” Compare with a tolerance, or test the strict reference.
It’s all or nothing per chain. One strict + in the middle of the fold restores the dependency chain at that point. Both the add and the multiply in the fold above are algebraic.
Iterator::sum stays strict. There’s no algebraic sum(), so write the fold (or the lanes) yourself.
const contexts work too (the methods are const since 1.98), but the docs promise nothing more about their compile-time results either.

title: RwLock Is Not a Faster Mutex: Lock Choice by Measurement, and Locks Across .await
text:
Thesis
“Reads don’t conflict, so use RwLock for read-heavy data” is half right. Readers don’t logically exclude each other. But every read() still writes to the lock: it adds one to a shared reader count, and dropping the guard subtracts one. In the standard library’s Linux implementation, that is a compare-exchange and a fetch_sub on one 32-bit word. With eight threads reading, that word’s cache line moves between cores on every acquisition. When the work inside the lock is tiny, the line transfer is the cost. The readers queue for the cache line just as Mutex users queue for the lock, and adding threads makes total throughput worse.
RwLock pays off only when the read-side critical section is long enough to hide that traffic. If the data really is read-mostly and the section is tiny, the answer is to stop sharing the written word: use an atomic, or give each reader its own lock (a “big-reader” lock). This chapter measures all of these.
Async code has a second lock rule: never hold a std::sync guard across an .await. The compiler enforces it only when the future has to be Send. On a current-thread runtime the same mistake compiles and deadlocks.

title: RwLock Is Not a Faster Mutex: Lock Choice by Measurement, and Locks Across .await
text:
Mental model



RwLock readers each do a CAS and a fetch_sub on one state word, so the cache line ping-pongs; measured ns per read for tiny and 0.4 µs sections; a big-reader lock with one aligned shard per reader; the async rule about std guards across .await


What one uncontended acquisition costs, from the standard library’s futex-based implementation (library/std/src/sys/sync/rwlock/futex.rs):








Operation
Atomic work on the shared word
Notes




RwLock::read()
load, then compare_exchange_weak(state, state + 1)
falls into read_contended() (spin, then futex wait) if the CAS fails or a writer is waiting


drop of a read guard
fetch_sub(1)
wakes a writer if this was the last reader


Mutex::lock() / drop
compare_exchange(0, 1) / swap(0)
waiters sleep on a futex


AtomicU64::load
none: a plain load
the line can stay shared in every core’s cache



The std source also fixes the priority policy. is_read_lockable returns false whenever the writers-waiting bit is set, and a comment in the same function calls these “writers, which have priority over readers”. So on Linux this RwLock is writer-preferring. That matters for the trap at the end of the chapter.

For read-mostly data with tiny sections, stop sharing the written word: an atomic for a scalar, or per-reader shards for larger data. Never take a second read guard on the same RwLock while you hold one. In async code, a std::sync::Mutex is fine as long as the guard lives in a block with no .await. If it must cross an .await, use tokio::sync::Mutex. Remember that the compiler catches this only where Send is required.

title: Tokio and Rayon: Separate Lanes for I/O and CPU Work
text:
Thesis
Tokio and Rayon are both thread pools, and both size themselves to “one thread per CPU” by default. They do opposite jobs. Tokio’s workers wait for many things at once and must come back to the scheduler quickly, at every .await. Rayon’s workers compute and are expected to stay busy until the job is done. Call par_iter() from inside an async handler and a Tokio worker stops polling futures until Rayon finishes. Do that on enough workers at the same time and the whole service freezes. Timers fire late, health checks time out, and connection pools look exhausted even though the database is idle.
The fix is not to avoid either library. Give each its own lane: async code hands CPU work to Rayon with rayon::spawn, awaits the result on a tokio::sync::oneshot channel, and limits how many batches are in flight with a Semaphore. This chapter measures the difference with a heartbeat timer, shows how the thread budget changes under a CPU limit, and covers the panic case that turns a bad request into a dead process.

title: Tokio and Rayon: Separate Lanes for I/O and CPU Work
text:
Mental model
 inline (wrong)                              separate lanes (right)

 Tokio worker 1: [handler ── par_iter ──────]   Tokio worker 1: [handler] await ... [reply]
 Tokio worker 2: [handler ── par_iter ──────]   Tokio worker 2: [tick][tick][tick][tick]
 ...  every worker blocked: no polling,                 │ rayon::spawn      ▲ oneshot
      timers late, sockets unread                       ▼                   │
                                                Rayon pool:   [evaluate ─────────────]







Fact
Consequence




A Tokio worker runs one task until it returns Poll::Pending
Synchronous work between two .awaits blocks every other task queued on that worker


par_iter() called outside the Rayon pool blocks the calling thread until the work is done
Inline Rayon in a handler is blocking code, however parallel it looks


rayon::spawn queues a job and returns immediately
The handler can .await a channel and give its worker back to Tokio


Both pools default to available_parallelism() threads
Two default pools mean 2× oversubscription. available_parallelism honours CPU affinity and cgroup quotas, so it shrinks under a container CPU limit


Rayon’s queue has no limit
Without a semaphore, a traffic burst becomes an ever-growing queue of CPU work

title: Tokio and Rayon: Separate Lanes for I/O and CPU Work
Tokio and Rayon: Separate Lanes for I/O and CPU Work
Tokio and Rayon: Separate Lanes for I/O and CPU Work
text:
The boring rule

Async handlers never call Rayon (or any long CPU loop) directly. They take a semaphore permit, rayon::spawn the work, and await a oneshot whose closed state is an error, not a panic. Both pools get explicit thread counts from the CPU request, Rayon has a panic handler, and small batches stay sequential.

title: Sans-IO Protocol Design: State Machines Without Sockets
text:
Thesis
A network protocol is a state machine. Sockets, timers, and async runtimes are drivers. Sans-IO (without I/O) keeps those layers apart: the protocol accepts bytes, clocks, and app intents through ordinary methods, and returns transmits and events through ordinary methods. No UdpSocket, no tokio::spawn, no Instant::now() hidden inside the library. The driver owns the socket and the clock; the protocol owns the rules.
That split buys three things operators and library authors care about. Tests run without ports or sleeps — feed a slice, advance a fake Instant, assert. The same crate works under Tokio, a blocking loop, or no_std with a custom timer. Composition becomes stacking machines (handle_input / poll_transmit) instead of colouring every call site async. This chapter builds a length-prefixed framer that way, proves it with byte-at-a-time reassembly and time travel, and names the traps that turn a clean machine into a busy-loop.

  │  (pure &mut self)   │◀── handle_input ── socket bytes
  │                     │◀── handle_timeout ─ Instant from driver
  │                     │  poll_event    ▶── app messages / errors
  │                     │  poll_timeout  ▶── next wake Instant

title: Cancel Safety: Dropping a Future Is Cancelling It
text:
Thesis
Async Rust has one universal cancellation protocol, and it is very easy to trigger: drop the future. A future is an inert state machine that only advances when it is polled. Once it is dropped it never runs again, and it stops at whichever .await it was parked on. You don’t need to call drop yourself. tokio::select! drops every branch that loses, tokio::time::timeout drops the future when the deadline fires, and try_join! drops the siblings of the first error. Because parents own their children, cancellation propagates down the whole call tree.
That makes two different questions worth asking about every .await:

Cancel safety is a local property of one future: if I drop it before it completes and create it again, is that a no-op? mpsc::Receiver::recv passes. read_exact and Sender::send(msg) fail.
Cancel correctness is a property of the whole system: if this future is dropped here, is any invariant, message, or cleanup lost? Dropping a cancel-unsafe future is a bug only when it breaks something you care about. Losing a half-read frame during shutdown is fine. Losing it in a select! loop is not.

This chapter reproduces the four bug shapes behind most production cancellation incidents and fixes each one. The fixes follow Rain’s “Cancelling Async Rust” (RustConf 2025) and Tokio’s own cancel-safety documentation.

title: async fn in Traits vs dyn Trait: Desugaring, Send Bounds and Boxing
text:
Thesis
Since Rust 1.75 you can write async fn directly inside a trait. That works well for static dispatch. It stops working at two points that every library author eventually reaches:

dyn Trait. A trait with an async fn is not dyn compatible, so Box<dyn Store> is a compile error.
Send. The future that async fn returns has a hidden type, and callers can’t add + Send to it. Generic code that spawns onto a multi-threaded runtime therefore can’t prove the future is thread-safe.

Both problems come from the same desugaring: async fn get(&self) -> u32 means fn get(&self) -> impl Future<Output = u32>. Each implementor returns its own, differently sized state machine. A vtable can’t hold “a function returning some unknown-size type”, and a bound you never wrote can’t be assumed.
This chapter reproduces all three compiler diagnostics on rustc 1.99.1 and fixes them with two moves: desugar by hand to add + Send, then add a boxed, dyn-compatible twin trait. The dynosaur and async-trait crates automate the same boxing. Everything here uses only std, including a ten-line block_on, so you can run it without Tokio.



Three shapes of an async trait: plain async fn (not dyn compatible, no Send), desugared impl Future + Send (static dispatch), boxed DynStore twin (dyn dispatch)

warning: use of `async fn` in public traits is discouraged as auto trait bounds cannot be specified

  |
2 |     async fn get(&self, key: u32) -> u32;
  |     ^^^^^
  |
  = note: you can suppress this lint if you plan to use the trait only in your own code, or do not care about auto traits like `Send` on the `Future`
  = note: `#[warn(async_fn_in_trait)]` on by default
help: you can alternatively desugar to a normal `fn` that returns `impl Future` and add any desired bounds such as `Send`, but these cannot be relaxed without a breaking API change
  |
2 -     async fn get(&self, key: u32) -> u32;
2 +     fn get(&self, key: u32) -> impl std::future::Future<Output = u32> + Send;
  |
The async_fn_in_trait lint fires only for public traits, because the problem belongs to downstream users. The suggestion it prints is fix number one.

title: C-Variadic Functions and VaList
text:
Thesis
Since Rust 1.99 (October 2026) you can define functions with a C variable argument list — unsafe extern "C" fn f(fmt: *const c_char, args: ...) — not just call foreign ones like printf. The ... parameter arrives as a core::ffi::VaList, which is layout- and ABI-compatible with the platform’s C va_list, so you can read arguments yourself or hand the whole list to a C v* function such as vsnprintf.
That closes a long-standing FFI gap: a Rust library can now implement a C header that contains void log(int level, const char *fmt, ...), sentinel-terminated APIs in the style of execl, or plugin callback tables that expect variadic slots — without a C shim file.
The feature is deliberately sharp. A variadic list carries no count and no types. Every read is an unsafe promise that the caller sent exactly what you are about to take. The job of this chapter is to make that promise small, explicit, and checked by the C compiler wherever possible.

title: C-Variadic Functions and VaList
text:
Mental model
C caller                       Rust callee (unsafe extern "C" fn f(fixed, ap: ...))
─────────                      ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
f(2, "x", 3.5f)                ap: VaList          ← va_start happens for you
   │  default argument               │
   │  promotions:                    ├─ ap.next_arg::<*const c_char>()   ← va_arg
   │   char/short → int              ├─ ap.next_arg::<c_double>()        ← va_arg
   │   float      → double           │
   ▼                                 ├─ ap.clone()                       ← va_copy
registers / stack per ABI            │
                                     └─ drop(ap)                         ← va_end







C
Rust 1.99




void f(int n, ...) (definition)
unsafe extern "C" fn f(n: c_int, mut ap: ...)


va_list ap; va_start(ap, n);
implicit — ap is the started VaList


va_arg(ap, int)
unsafe { ap.next_arg::<c_int>() }


va_copy(dst, src)
let dst = src.clone();


va_end(ap)
Drop of the VaList


void vf(int n, va_list ap)
unsafe fn vf(n: c_int, ap: VaList<'_>)



Rules the compiler enforces:

The definition must be unsafe. Callers cannot be checked, so the function is unsafe to call.
ABI must be "C" or "C-unwind" for a Rust-bodied definition (other ABIs are only allowed for declarations in extern blocks, or naked functions written in assembly).
The ... parameter needs a name in a definition (args: ...), and it must be last.
Only promotion-safe types can be read. next_arg::<T>() requires the (nightly-only) trait VaArgSafe; on stable you just use the concrete types it is implemented for: c_int/c_uint and wider integers, c_double, and raw pointers. f32, i8, u16, and bool are rejected because C never passes them through ... unpromoted.

Rules the compiler cannot enforce: how many arguments there are, and what type each one has. Those come from a protocol — a count, a format string, or a sentinel — that you document in the # Safety section and, ideally, encode in the C header.

title: C-Variadic Functions and VaList
C-Variadic Functions and VaList
text:
The trap
Treating next_arg as if it were type-checked. It is a raw read guided only by your protocol. Every one of these is undefined behaviour, and none produces a compile error in the callee:

Reading past the end. There is no length; next_arg on an exhausted list reads whatever is in the next register or stack slot. A missing sentinel in Case 2 walks off into garbage pointers.
Reading the wrong type. Caller passes long long, you read c_int; caller passes double, you read a pointer. The VaList docs allow only compatible types: identical types, same-size integers whose value fits both, compatible pointers, or *const c_void ↔︎ *const u8/i8.
Trusting integer widths across platforms. c_long is 64-bit on Linux x86_64 and 32-bit on Windows x86_64. Read c_long when the C side passes long, not i64. The VaArgSafe docs say implementations for i32/usize “shouldn’t be relied upon directly”; spell the C type.
Re-reading a consumed list. After vsnprintf(…, ap) the list is spent; use ap.clone() before the first consumer if you need two passes.
Panicking out of an extern "C" function. A panic that reaches an extern "C" boundary aborts the process. If unwinding through C is genuinely intended, use "C-unwind"; otherwise catch and convert errors to return codes, as rlog does with its None branch.
Calling your own variadic from Rust. Rust callers get none of the C header’s format checking. Give Rust code a normal, safe function (fn log(level: Level, msg: &str)) and keep the variadic entry point for C.

title: C-Variadic Functions and VaList
text:
The boring rule

A C-variadic function in Rust is a thin, unsafe, #[unsafe(no_mangle)] door for C callers. It reads arguments only under a documented protocol — a count, a format string handed to libc’s v* functions, or a NULL sentinel — reads only C-spelled promoted types (c_int, c_uint, c_long, c_double, pointers), clones before any second pass, never unwinds through extern "C", and ships with a C header carrying format(printf, …) or sentinel so the caller’s compiler checks what the callee cannot.

Checklist before merging:

# Safety section states the exact protocol (how many, which types, how the list ends).
Real formatting is delegated to vsnprintf/vfprintf; you do not reimplement % parsing.
Every read type is a core::ffi C type or a raw pointer.
The C header has __attribute__((format(printf, N, M))) or __attribute__((sentinel)), and CI builds C callers with -Werror=format.
Rust-side callers use a safe non-variadic API instead.

FFI bool miscompile on x86_64 (Rust 1.99.0 → 1.99.1)
Rust’s bool is not a C int. Across the extern "C" boundary it must follow the platform ABI: on x86-64 SysV, a _Bool / bool return is a byte whose bits 1–7 are zero (bits above that are undefined). If the compiler forgets to zero-extend, a C caller that reads the return as bool can observe values like 16 instead of 0 or 1—and then every if (flag) in C becomes a landmine.
Rust 1.99.0 shipped a regression that dropped that zero-extension for FFI bool returns on several x86_64 targets. 1.99.1 (2026-10-15) restored it. This chapter is the incident report you want next to the FFI chapter: what broke, how to see it in a register dump, who is affected, and what to do on a pinned toolchain.

Per the issue and write-ups circulating with 1.99.1:

Targets: x86_64 SysV-style environments (Linux, musl, FreeBSD, Android, many bare-metal x86_64 configs). aarch64 / loongarch64 reproductions in the report masked correctly.
Surface: Rust functions with extern "C" (or other C-like ABIs) that return bool, especially when compiled with optimizations so LLVM folds the compare into a raw register move.
Not required: unsafe in the callee body beyond FFI—the export itself is the hazard. Callers in C/bindgen glue are where symptoms show up (wrong branch, wrong printf, corrupted flag packing).

If you ship a cdylib / staticlib consumed by C/C++/other languages, inventory -> bool at the boundary.

title: FFI bool miscompile on x86_64 (Rust 1.99.0 → 1.99.1)
text:
Case 3 — Mitigations

Upgrade: rustup update stable → 1.99.1 or newer, then rebuild all Rust artifacts that cross FFI (don’t assume an old .so is fine).
Temporary pin: Stay on 1.98.x until you can move, if 1.99.0 is already in CI.
ABI hygiene: Return u8 (0/1) or c_int at the boundary and convert explicitly:

#[unsafe(no_mangle)]
pub unsafe extern "C" fn rust_fn_returning_u8(flags: u8) -> u8 {
    u8::from((flags & 0x1) == 0x1)
}

Test in CI: Keep a C (or cc crate) smoke test that passes a non-0/1 pattern in the low byte’s upper bits and asserts a clean 0/1 out—exactly the repro above.

title: Safe Rust UAF via covariant field assignment (rust#164250)
text:
Safe Rust UAF via covariant field assignment (rust#164250)
Rust’s type system is supposed to make use-after-free impossible in safe code. Issue rust-lang/rust#164250 (opened 2026-10-13, labels I-unsound, P-high, A-variance, A-borrow-checker) shows a counterexample: no unsafe keyword, yet a Drop impl can observe a dangling reference. A minimized form has compiled since Rust 1.4 (2015). This chapter is the incident card next to the unsafe / FFI chapters: what breaks, how to reproduce on current stable, and what to audit in your own crates — not a claim that everyday application code is doomed.

title: Safe Rust UAF via covariant field assignment (rust#164250)
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

State the bug in one sentence: lifetime bounds on a type are not fully enforced when a covariant field is assigned after construction
Reproduce the MyType / Drop smuggling pattern on rustc 1.99.0
Separate “malicious Drop” exploitability from accidental UAF in ordinary code (per the Types Team note on the issue)
Know where to watch for fixes (Types Team / Project Zero work; do not “patch” this in user code with unsafe)

title: Safe Rust UAF via covariant field assignment (rust#164250)
text:
Thesis

If the compiler accepts a shorter-lived reference into a field whose type promised a longer lifetime, Drop runs with a lie. Safe code can then read freed stack memory — the soundness bug is in the type checker, not in your unsafe blocks.

title: Safe Rust UAF via covariant field assignment (rust#164250)
text:
Mental model
  struct MyType<'a, 'b: 'a, 'c>(&'c mut &'a str, &'b str);
       │                              │
       │                              └─ field 1: covariant in 'b
       └─ Drop assumes 'b: 'a (and related bounds) still hold

  construction:  MyType(&mut me_out, "")     // '' is 'static-ish / long enough
  later assign:  q.1 = &local_string;        // shorter 'b sneaks in
  scope ends:    Drop runs → *me_out = dangling
  after scope:   print(me_out) → UAF







Piece
Role




Covariance on a field
Allows treating a shorter lifetime as a longer one when unifying / assigning


Lifetime bounds on the struct ('b: 'a, 'a: 'static, …)
Documented intent; not re-checked thoroughly on field assignment in this bug


Drop
Runs while the type system still believes the long lifetime


No unsafe in the repro
The unsoundness is accepting the program, not an explicit transmute



The Types Team note on the issue: this would be P-critical on novelty grounds, but an 11-year-old hole that stayed unnoticed is hard to hit by accident; exploiting it generally needs an intentionally malicious Drop. Treat production risk as real but not “rewrite everything tomorrow”.

title: Life before main: .init_array, #[used], and why LazyLock is usually the answer
section: The mechanism, from the ELF spec
text:
The mechanism, from the ELF spec
The System V gABI defines SHT_INIT_ARRAY as “an array of pointers to initialization functions”. Its dynamic-section chapter says those functions are executed by the dynamic linker in the order their addresses appear in the array. The .fini_array entries run in reverse order. So a constructor is nothing more than one pointer-sized value that lands in that section.
Rust gives you the two tools you need:

link_section “specifies the section of the object file that a function or static’s content will be placed into.”
used “forces a static to be kept in the output object file … even if it’s never used or referenced by any other item in the crate.”

title: Life before main: .init_array, #[used], and why LazyLock is usually the answer
Life before main: .init_array, #[used], and why LazyLock is usually the answer
text:
Real output (rustc 1.99.1, x86_64 Linux, glibc 2.41)
$ rustc --edition 2024 -O before.rs -o before && ./before
[early_init] running before main
main: INIT_CALLS = 1
main: before touching CONFIG
[LazyLock] initialising on first use
main: CONFIG = mode=fast
main: CONFIG again = mode=fast
The constructor ran once, before main’s first line. The LazyLock ran once, inside main, on first dereference, and not again on the second.

title: Life before main: .init_array, #[used], and why LazyLock is usually the answer
text:
Drop #[used] and it silently disappears
Here is the same file with only the #[used] line removed:
$ rustc --edition 2024 -O nouse.rs -o nouse
warning: function `early_init` is never used
warning: static `EARLY_INIT` is never used
warning: function `libc_write` is never used
warning: 3 warnings emitted
$ ./nouse
main: INIT_CALLS = 0
main: before touching CONFIG
[LazyLock] initialising on first use
main: CONFIG = mode=fast
main: CONFIG again = mode=fast
It still compiles, it still runs, and the constructor is gone. The section headers show why:
$ readelf -S before | grep -A1 init_array
  [22] .init_array       INIT_ARRAY       0000000000050e48  0004ee48
       0000000000000018  0000000000000000 WAo       0     0     8
$ readelf -S nouse | grep -A1 init_array
  [22] .init_array       INIT_ARRAY       0000000000050db8  0004edb8
       0000000000000010  0000000000000000 WAo       0     0     8
Without #[used] the array holds 0x10 bytes (two 8-byte pointers that were already there, contributed by the C startup objects and the standard library — I did not trace which is which). With it, the array holds 0x18 bytes, so our entry is the third pointer. Nothing references EARLY_INIT, so the compiler treats it as dead and drops it. The only clue is the dead-code warning. If you treat warnings as noise, or #![allow(dead_code)] is set at crate level, nothing tells you.
Two more details from the reference: #[used] only keeps the item in the object file, and “the linker, however, is still free to remove it.” In this binary the linker kept it, because .init_array is a section the linker preserves. With a custom section name and --gc-sections, you would need to check again.
If you dump the raw bytes with readelf -x .init_array before, they are all zeros. This is a position-independent executable, so the pointers are filled in at load time by R_X86_64_RELATIVE relocations, not stored in the file. Don’t conclude the entry is missing from the hex dump; count the section size instead.

title: Life before main: .init_array, #[used], and why LazyLock is usually the answer
section: Edition 2024: link_section is an unsafe attribute
text:
Edition 2024: link_section is an unsafe attribute
In the 2024 edition, export_name, link_section and no_mangle must be written as unsafe(...). These attributes control linking in a global symbol namespace, and getting them wrong can cause UB from otherwise safe code. The plain spelling is a hard error:
$ rustc --edition 2024 plain.rs
error: unsafe attribute used without unsafe
  --> plain.rs:19:3
   |
19 | #[link_section = ".init_array"]
   |   ^^^^^^^^^^^^ usage of unsafe attribute
   |
help: wrap the attribute in `unsafe(...)`
Under --edition 2021 the same file builds, and the constructor runs ([early_init] running before main). Migrating to 2024 adds the unsafe(...) marker; it doesn’t change what the attribute does.
The unsafe marker is honest. Code in .init_array runs:

before std has finished setting up its runtime (for example, the main thread’s name and the stack-overflow handlers on Unix);
in an order you only partly control, across crates and shared libraries;
with no way to catch a panic. Unwinding out of an extern "C" fn aborts the process.

title: Life before main: .init_array, #[used], and why LazyLock is usually the answer
section: What to do instead, most of the time
text:
What to do instead, most of the time
std::sync::LazyLock (stable since 1.80) covers almost every “I need a global initialised once” case:

it runs on first access, inside main, with the full standard library available;
it is thread-safe;
it needs no linker, unsafe attribute, or platform-specific section name.

The output above shows the difference in timing: before touching CONFIG prints before the initialiser does.
Reach for a real constructor only when something has to happen before any user code. Examples include registering with a plugin host that dlopens your cdylib, or self-registering test cases or types across crates, which is what inventory-style crates are for. Even then, use ctor rather than the hand-rolled version. It knows each platform’s section name (its docs show .init_array on Linux, __DATA,__mod_init_func on Apple, .CRT$XCU on Windows), and in its 1.x API it makes you write #[ctor(unsafe)] to acknowledge the same caveats.

title: Life before main: .init_array, #[used], and why LazyLock is usually the answer
text:
Checklist

#[used] on the static, or it is silently removed.
#[unsafe(link_section = ".init_array")] on edition 2024.
extern "C" fn() signature, with no arguments and no panics.
Body uses only libc-level calls and atomics: no println!, allocation-heavy work, or thread spawning.
Verified by section size (readelf -S), not by the zero-filled hex dump.
Asked first whether LazyLock solves it, and the answer is usually yes.

title: MSRV in practice: rust-version and the MSRV-aware resolver
text:
MSRV in practice: rust-version and the MSRV-aware resolver
Your crate’s minimum supported Rust version (MSRV) is not just a property of your own code. It is a property of the whole dependency graph that Cargo.lock pins. One cargo update can pull in a transitive dependency, two or three levels down, that needs a newer compiler than you promised. Your source is unchanged, and the build breaks for everyone on the older toolchain. This chapter shows that break with real crates, then fixes it with the tools Cargo has shipped since 1.84: package.rust-version, resolver "3" (the MSRV-aware resolver, default in edition 2024), cargo add’s MSRV awareness, --ignore-rust-version, and --locked.

title: MSRV in practice: rust-version and the MSRV-aware resolver
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Explain why a dependency with an old MSRV can still break your MSRV build
Read Cargo’s requires Rust 1.xx annotations and its “rustc … is not supported” error
Switch a project to the MSRV-aware resolver and see what it downgrades and why
Tell when the resolver cannot help (your own version requirement is too new)
Make CI check the MSRV with the committed lockfile

title: MSRV in practice: rust-version and the MSRV-aware resolver
text:
Thesis

rust-version is a promise about the build graph, not just your crate. Since Cargo 1.84 the resolver can keep that promise for you. With resolver "3" it prefers dependency versions whose own rust-version fits yours. It only does that if you opt in (edition 2024, resolver = "3", or config), if dependencies declare rust-version, and if your version requirements leave it room.

text:
Mental model
  Cargo.toml requirement      →   resolver picks a version    →   Cargo.lock    →   rustc checks every
  url = "2.5"                     (newest that matches;            pins it          package's rust-version
                                   resolver 3: newest that                          at build time
                                   ALSO fits your rust-version)



One package with rust-version 1.85; resolver 2 picks transitive versions needing Rust 1.86/1.88 and fails, resolver 3 picks older compatible ones and builds










Knob
Where
Effect




package.rust-version = "1.85"
Cargo.toml
Your MSRV. Cargo refuses to build on an older rustc. cargo add and resolver "3" use it to choose versions


resolver = "3"
[package] or [workspace]
Default for edition 2024. Sets incompatible-rust-versions = "fallback"


resolver.incompatible-rust-versions
.cargo/config.toml / CARGO_RESOLVER_INCOMPATIBLE_RUST_VERSIONS
allow (old behaviour) or fallback (prefer compatible, use incompatible only if nothing else matches). Respected since Cargo 1.84


--ignore-rust-version
CLI
Build or resolve as if no rust-version were set


--locked
CLI
Fail instead of changing Cargo.lock



“Your Rust version” for the resolver is the workspace’s rust-version. If that is unset, Cargo uses the toolchain you are running (Case 5).

uuid = { version = "1.26.1", features = ["v4"] }

--- now ask for a version that only exists for newer Rust
    Updating crates.io index

    Updating uuid v1.26.1 -> v1.28.0 (requires Rust 1.89.0)

error: rustc 1.85.1 is not supported by the following package:

`cargo update <name>@<current-ver> --precise <compatible-ver>`

cargo add chose 1.26.1 and said why (ignoring uuid@1.28.0 (which requires rustc 1.89.0)). Once the manifest says "1.28", no version that satisfies the requirement fits Rust 1.85. The resolver’s fallback policy is documented to pick an incompatible version instead of failing resolution, so cargo update succeeded, and cargo build refused. The fix is in Cargo.toml: lower the requirement or raise rust-version. The resolver cannot fix it.

title: MSRV in practice: rust-version and the MSRV-aware resolver
section: Case 4 — Your own rust-version, the escape hatch, and --locked
text:
Case 4 — Your own rust-version, the escape hatch, and --locked
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-04-own-msrv.sh — rust-version also guards your own package
set -uo pipefail
cd /tmp/msrv-lab
sed -i 's/^uuid = .*/uuid = { version = "1.26", features = ["v4"] }/' Cargo.toml
cargo update -q -p uuid --precise 1.26.1 2>&1
sed -i 's/^rust-version = "1.85"/rust-version = "1.90"/' Cargo.toml
echo '--- claim a newer MSRV than this toolchain'
cargo build -q 2>&1 | head -4
echo "[cargo build exit ${PIPESTATUS[0]}]"
echo '--- the escape hatch (use when you know why)'
cargo build -q --ignore-rust-version 2>&1 && echo '[build ok with --ignore-rust-version]'
sed -i 's/^rust-version = "1.90"/rust-version = "1.85"/' Cargo.toml

echo '--- CI: the lockfile is the contract'
cargo build -q --locked 2>&1 && echo '[--locked build ok]'
sed -i 's/^url = "2.5"/url = "=2.5.4"/' Cargo.toml
cargo build -q --locked 2>&1 | head -3
echo "[--locked build exit ${PIPESTATUS[0]}]"
--- claim a newer MSRV than this toolchain
error: rustc 1.85.1 is not supported by the following package:
  msrv-lab@0.1.0 requires rustc 1.90

[cargo build exit 101]
--- the escape hatch (use when you know why)
[build ok with --ignore-rust-version]
--- CI: the lockfile is the contract
[--locked build ok]
error: the lock file /tmp/msrv-lab/Cargo.lock needs to be updated but --locked was passed to prevent this
If you want to try to generate the lock file without accessing the network, remove the --locked flag and use --offline instead.
[--locked build exit 101]

Claiming rust-version = "1.90" makes Cargo reject your own package on 1.85.1 with a clear message, before rustc can fail on some syntax error deep in your code. That is what the field is for.
--ignore-rust-version builds anyway. Use it when you know the newer feature is behind a cfg you do not hit, not as a habit.
--locked makes the committed lockfile the contract. When the manifest and the lockfile disagree, CI fails instead of silently resolving a new graph. That is how you stop a CI run from picking up a transitive update that nobody reviewed.

section: Case 5 — No rust-version? Then your toolchain is the MSRV
text:
Case 5 — No rust-version? Then your toolchain is the MSRV
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-05-no-msrv.sh — no rust-version at all: what does resolver "3" compare against?
set -uo pipefail
cd /tmp/msrv-lab
sed -i 's/^url = "=2.5.4"/url = "2.5"/; /^rust-version = /d' Cargo.toml
grep -E '^(edition|rust-version|resolver)' Cargo.toml
rm -f Cargo.lock
cargo generate-lockfile 2>&1 | grep -E 'Locking|uuid|icu_normalizer '
cargo build -q 2>&1 && echo '[build ok on rustc 1.85.1]'
edition = "2021"          # resolver "2": rust-version of deps is ignored
resolver = "3"             # default for edition 2024; needs Cargo 1.84+
     Locking 53 packages to latest Rust 1.85.1 compatible versions
      Adding icu_normalizer v2.1.1 (available: v2.3.0, requires Rust 1.88)
      Adding uuid v1.26.1 (available: v1.28.0, requires Rust 1.89.0)
[build ok on rustc 1.85.1]
With rust-version removed, resolver "3" resolved against “Rust 1.85.1”, the toolchain running cargo. That is convenient on one machine and a trap on a team. A developer on 1.99 and a CI runner on 1.85 generate different lockfiles from the same manifest. Declare rust-version and the result no longer depends on who ran cargo update.

title: MSRV in practice: rust-version and the MSRV-aware resolver
section: Case 6 — Check the MSRV in CI (configuration, not run here)
text:
Case 6 — Check the MSRV in CI (configuration, not run here)
This needs a second toolchain (rustup toolchain install), which this box does not have, so it was not run. It is the pattern the Cargo book’s “Rust version” chapter and its CI guide describe: verify the MSRV with the lockfile you ship.
# .github/workflows/msrv.yml — build the committed Cargo.lock on the declared MSRV
name: msrv
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  msrv:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - run: rustup toolchain install 1.85 --profile minimal
      - run: cargo +1.85 check --locked --all-targets
Pair it with a normal job on the latest stable, so you also see breakage that a newer compiler would catch. For libraries, remember that downstream users do not use your Cargo.lock. Their resolver, their rust-version and their toolchain decide what they get. The rust-version field on every crate in the graph is what lets their resolver choose well.

title: MSRV in practice: rust-version and the MSRV-aware resolver
text:
The trap
The trap is reading MSRV as “the oldest compiler that compiles my code”. You test once on the old toolchain, it works, and you ship. Weeks later a routine cargo update, or a fresh clone without a lockfile, pulls icu_normalizer 2.3.0 three levels down, and the MSRV build fails with no change to your code. The two usual fixes make it worse. Pinning the transitive crate with = in your own Cargo.toml freezes it for every downstream user. Dropping rust-version makes Cargo resolve against whichever toolchain happens to run, so the lockfile changes from one machine to the next.

title: MSRV in practice: rust-version and the MSRV-aware resolver
text:
The boring rule

Declare package.rust-version. Use resolver "3" (edition 2024 gives it to you). Let cargo add choose versions. Commit Cargo.lock for applications and build with --locked in CI. Keep one CI job on the declared MSRV and one on latest stable. When a dependency needs a newer compiler, decide deliberately: raise rust-version (a minor-version bump per the Cargo book) or keep the older dependency. Don’t hand-pin transitive crates.
