text: build.rs Runs As You: Build Scripts and the Supply Chain

title: build.rs Runs As You: Build Scripts and the Supply Chain
text:
Thesis
Adding a dependency doesn’t just add code to your binary. It adds code that runs on your machine at build time. The Cargo reference puts it plainly: placing a file named build.rs in a package root “will cause Cargo to compile that script and execute it just before building the package” (Build Scripts). Procedural macros are the same: they are compiler plugins that run inside rustc. Neither is sandboxed. They run with your user, your environment, your files and your network.
That is why typosquatting works so well against Rust developers: a crate named almost like proc-macro2 only has to be built to act. This chapter shows exactly when that code runs, using a harmless look-alike crate, and what a simple sandbox does and doesn’t stop.



When does dependency code run on your machine?

title: build.rs Runs As You: Build Scripts and the Supply Chain
build.rs Runs As You: Build Scripts and the Supply Chain
text:
When it runs
#!/bin/sh
cd "$(dirname "$0")/app"
set -x
cargo metadata --format-version 1 --offline > /dev/null; ls /tmp/buildrs-was-here
cargo check --offline 2>&1 | grep -v "^ *Finished\|^ *Checking\|^ *Compiling"
cat /tmp/buildrs-was-here
rm -f /tmp/buildrs-was-here; cargo clean -q
unshare -rn cargo check --offline 2>&1 | grep -v "^ *Finished\|^ *Checking\|^ *Compiling"
cat /tmp/buildrs-was-here
Output with cargo 1.99.1 on Linux:
+ cargo metadata --format-version 1 --offline
+ ls /tmp/buildrs-was-here
ls: cannot access '/tmp/buildrs-was-here': No such file or directory
+ cargo check --offline
+ grep -v ^ *Finished\|^ *Checking\|^ *Compiling
warning: proc-macro-two@0.1.0: build.rs ran as uid 1000: saw 111 env vars, 0 entries in ~/.ssh; network: connected to 1.1.1.1:443
+ cat /tmp/buildrs-was-here
build.rs ran as uid 1000: saw 111 env vars, 0 entries in ~/.ssh; network: connected to 1.1.1.1:443
+ rm -f /tmp/buildrs-was-here
+ cargo clean -q
+ unshare -rn cargo check --offline
+ grep -v ^ *Finished\|^ *Checking\|^ *Compiling
warning: proc-macro-two@0.1.0: build.rs ran as uid 0: saw 111 env vars, 0 entries in ~/.ssh; network: Network is unreachable (os error 101)
+ cat /tmp/buildrs-was-here
build.rs ran as uid 0: saw 111 env vars, 0 entries in ~/.ssh; network: Network is unreachable (os error 101)
What happened:

cargo metadata didn’t run it. Resolving the dependency graph is safe, so the marker file doesn’t exist yet.
cargo check ran it, even though check produces no binary. The build script ran as uid 1000 (the developer), saw all 111 environment variables, reached 1.1.1.1:443 on the internet, and wrote /tmp/buildrs-was-here. A real attack would have sent the variables instead of counting them.
Editors do the same. rust-analyzer’s rust-analyzer.cargo.buildScripts.enable defaults to true (“Run build scripts (build.rs) for more precise code analysis”), and proc-macro support implies it (configuration). Opening a cloned repository in your editor can be enough.
A namespace sandbox is partial. Under unshare -rn (a new user namespace mapping you to uid 0, plus an empty network namespace), the connection fails with Network is unreachable. The script still read the environment and still wrote to /tmp on the host. To contain the filesystem too, you need a container or VM with only the source tree mounted, or a dedicated build user.

title: build.rs Runs As You: Build Scripts and the Supply Chain
text:
Defences, in order of payoff

Watch what enters Cargo.lock. Most attacks need a new package name: a typo, a look-alike, or a dependency confusion. Review lockfile diffs in PRs like code, and build in CI with cargo build --locked so nothing is resolved silently.
Audit before you trust. cargo-vet records which crate versions “have been audited by a trusted entity” and fails CI for unaudited ones. cargo-deny can ban crates, restrict sources to crates.io or known git hosts, and check RustSec advisories.
Vendor for hermetic builds. cargo vendor plus --offline makes the build use exactly the reviewed sources.
Sandbox untrusted builds, including the first build of a cloned repository and any editor session in one. Cut both the network and the host filesystem, as the namespace experiment above shows.
Keep secrets out of build environments. A build job that doesn’t need a publish token shouldn’t have one. Everything in env::vars() is readable by every build script in the graph.

title: build.rs Runs As You: Build Scripts and the Supply Chain
text:
Takeaways

build.rs and proc macros run at build time, as you, with full access. cargo check and your editor trigger them, while cargo metadata doesn’t.
A look-alike name is the whole attack. Lockfile review, --locked, and cargo-vet or cargo-deny stop it before it builds.
Sandboxes have to cover the network and the filesystem: unshare -rn alone left the host file write intact.

Thesis
On 2026-04-13 the Servo project published servo 0.1.0 on crates.io — the first release of the engine as a library, not only as the servoshell demo browser. The 0.1 version number is deliberate: the team has not defined what 1.0 means yet, but the bump signals growing confidence that the embedding API is usable for real embedders. Monthly crates keep moving (by late 2026 the crate line includes 0.7.x regular releases plus a parallel 0.1.x LTS line). This chapter teaches the mental model of embedding Servo: what the crate is for, what 0.1 vs LTS vs monthly means, and which build/feature knobs matter — without downloading the engine’s enormous dependency graph in the book lab.

Core Principles
Looking back over our journey, three fundamental engineering principles define idiomatic Rust:

Safety is an Asset, Not a Constraint: The borrow checker is an automated proof assistant ensuring thread and memory safety.

Where Rust Shines
Rust delivers unmatched value in: - High-performance network proxies, database engines, and storage systems. - Operating system kernels, drivers, and hypervisors. - Low-latency financial trading platforms. - WebAssembly client-side computational modules and edge serverless workers. - Embedded firmware and safety-critical medical and automotive controllers.

title: Where Rust May Not Be the Best Fit
text:
Where Rust May Not Be the Best Fit
Rust may introduce unnecessary friction for: - Disposable one-off scripts where Python or Bash finishes the job in minutes. - Rapidly churning early-stage UI prototypes where types and domain models change hourly. - Systems where memory footprint and latency do not matter and teams already possess deep expertise in managed languages.

title: Continuing Your Journey
text:
Continuing Your Journey
To continue deepening your Rust mastery: - Read The Rust Reference and The Rustonomicon for deep language semantics and unsafe invariants. - Explore open-source projects on crates.io to observe production architectures. - Contribute bug fixes and documentation improvements to the community.

title: Final Thoughts
text:
Final Thoughts
Rust changes the way you think about programming. Even when writing Go, C, or Python, the habits ingrained by Rust—thinking carefully about ownership, data sharing, mutability, and error handling—will make you a vastly more rigorous systems engineer.
Welcome to the community, and build fearless software.
